payload.title: Acid–base reasoning
payload.fullNote:
Brønsted acids donate H+ and bases accept it. Lewis acids accept an electron pair; Lewis bases donate one. In a coordinate covalent bond, both shared electrons originate from the donor; the resulting bond is still covalent. For HA + B ⇌ A− + BH+, K ≈ 10^[pKa(BH+) − pKa(HA)] when the pKa values use comparable conditions.

Amphoteric species can act as acids or bases, depending on the partner. Water can accept H+ to form H3O+ or donate H+ to form OH−; bicarbonate can likewise gain or lose a proton.

payload.title: Acid–base reasoning
payload.fullNote: Lower pKa means stronger acid. Stabilize the conjugate base to increase acidity. Across a comparable row, electronegativity can stabilize negative charge; down a group, weaker H–X bonds and charge dispersion can dominate. Compare like structures and conditions, rather than applying a single trend everywhere.

visualCard.title: ARIO Conjugate Base Stability & pH vs. pKa Speciation
visualCard.prompt: How are you evaluating acid strength or protonation state?

items.label: Comparing Two Acids Without pKa Values
items.outcome: Deprotonate Both → Apply ARIO to Conjugate Base A⁻
items.text: More stable conjugate base = stronger acid! Across a row electronegativity wins (OH > NH₂); down a column size wins (I⁻ > F⁻, so HI > HF).

items.label: Comparing pH to pKa in Solution
items.outcome: pH < pKa → Protonated (HA); pH > pKa → Deprotonated (A⁻)
items.text: If pH is 2 units above pKa, the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is 10² = 100:1 (99% deprotonated).

items.label: Inductive Effect (CF₃COOH vs CH₃COOH)
items.outcome: EWGs Pull Electron Density → ↓ pKa (Stronger Acid)
items.text: Inductive withdrawal falls off rapidly with distance (α-Cl > β-Cl > γ-Cl) and follows electronegativity (F > Cl > Br > I).

visualCard.title: Thinking HF Is Stronger Than HI or That Electron-Withdrawing Groups Raise pKa

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Saying HF is stronger than HI because F is more electronegative, or saying EWGs "increase pKa".

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Down a periodic column, atomic radius dominates (I⁻ spreads negative charge over a huge volume, so HI pKa −10 ≪ HF pKa 3.2); stronger acids have LOWER pKa!

payload.title: Nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups
payload.fullNote: A nucleophile supplies an electron pair to an electrophile. A leaving group takes the bonding pair when it departs. Stable weak bases usually make better leaving groups. Protonation can turn poor leaving group OH− into neutral water.

visualCard.title: Nucleophiles, Electrophiles, Leaving Group Ability & Solvent Effects

items.label: Nucleophilicity vs. Basicity
items.text: Basicity is thermodynamic affinity for H⁺; nucleophilicity is kinetic attack rate at carbon (sensitive to steric bulk and solvent).

items.label: Protic vs. Polar Aprotic Solvents
items.text: Protic solvents H-bond tightly to small F⁻ (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻); polar aprotic solvents leave F⁻ bare and reactive (F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻).

items.label: Leaving Group Rule (Weak Base = Good LG)
items.text: The best leaving groups are stable weak bases whose conjugate acids have pKa < 0 (TsO⁻, MsO⁻, I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, H₂O).

comparison: TsO⁻, I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, H₂O (never HO⁻ in SN1/SN2)

payload.title: Nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups
payload.fullNote:
Find electron-rich donor → electron-poor acceptor → possible leaving group. Curved arrows start at electrons, not positive charges.

Compare nucleophilicity using charge, reacting-atom identity, steric access, and solvent. For a similar reacting atom, an anion is often more nucleophilic than its neutral conjugate acid. Across comparable atoms in a row, lower electronegativity often favors donation. Bulky donors are hindered in SN2. Protic solvation and polarizability can reverse simple basicity-based trends down a group; polar aprotic conditions often favor anionic SN2 nucleophiles.

visualCard.title: Strong Nucleophile vs. Bulky Base & Leaving Group Activation
visualCard.prompt: What reagent or leaving group role are you diagnosing?

items.label: Small Charged Anion (CN⁻, RS⁻, I⁻, N₃⁻, RO⁻)
items.text: High polarizability or localized negative charge with minimal steric bulk favors substitution attack at δ+ carbon.

items.label: Sterically Hindered Base (t-BuO⁻, LDA, DBU)
items.outcome: Strong Base Only → Forces E2 Elimination!
items.text: Too bulky to reach a backside carbon σ* orbital; plucks an exposed β-proton instead.

items.label: Poor Leaving Group (–OH, –OR, –NH₂)
items.text: Strong bases (HO⁻, RO⁻, H₂N⁻) never leave directly in SN1/SN2; convert –OH into H₂O or –OTs first!

payload.title: Nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups
payload.fullNote: A carbonyl oxygen is electron rich while its carbon is electron poor. A positive charge is not required for electrophilicity. For comparable neutral acyl derivatives in nucleophilic acyl substitution, anhydrides are generally more reactive than esters, and esters more reactive than amides. A free carboxylic acid can instead protonate a basic nucleophile; protonation, activation and the leaving group prevent a universal acid/ester ranking.

visualCard.title: Kicking Out Hydroxide (HO⁻) Directly in SN1/SN2 or Reversing Curved Arrows

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Drawing ROH + Br⁻ → RBr + HO⁻ directly, or drawing a curved arrow from the electrophile C⁺ to the nucleophile.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Curved arrows ALWAYS start at an electron source (lone pair or π bond) and point to an electron sink; protonate –OH to –OH₂⁺ before displacement.

visualCard.title: Biological Leaving Groups (ATP Pyrophosphate PP_i) & SAM Methylation

items.label: ATP & Pyrophosphate (PP_i)
items.text: Enzymes phosphorylate alcohols to convert poor –OH leaving groups into resonance-stabilized phosphate/pyrophosphate leaving groups.

items.label: Cysteine Thiolate (RS⁻)
items.text: Sulfur’s large, polarizable 3p valence shell makes Cys–S⁻ a far faster nucleophile than Ser–O⁻ in protic water.

items.label: S-Adenosylmethionine (SAM)
items.text: Positively charged R₂S⁺–CH₃ acts as a prime biological leaving group for SN2 methyl transfer.

payload.title: SN1 vs. SN2
payload.fullNote: SN2 is concerted backside attack: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile], with geometric inversion. Methyl and unhindered primary centers are favorable. SN1 ionizes to a carbocation: rate = k[substrate]; tertiary, allylic, and benzylic stabilization can help.

visualCard.formula: SN2 Rate = k [Substrate][Nucleophile] (Bimolecular)     |     SN1 Rate = k [Substrate] (Unimolecular)

items.label: SN2 Stereochemistry & Substrate

items.label: SN1 Stereochemistry & Rearrangement
items.text: Rate-determining LG loss forms a planar sp² carbocation (3°/allylic/benzylic > 2°); attacked from both faces (racemization) and can rearrange!

payload.title: Organic oxidation and reduction
payload.fullNote: Oxidation of carbon usually increases bonds to O/N/halogens or decreases C–H bonds. Reduction does the reverse. C–C bonds contribute zero to carbon oxidation state. PCC under anhydrous conditions can oxidize a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Aqueous acidic CrO3 or dichromate (Na2Cr2O7/K2Cr2O7), or suitable KMnO4 conditions, can oxidize a primary alcohol further to a carboxylic acid; substrate and conditions determine the outcome.

visualCard.title: Organic Oxidation States & Chemoselective Oxidizing / Reducing Reagents

items.label: Carbon Oxidation Ladder
items.text: Alkane (−4 in CH₄) → Alcohol/Alkene → Aldehyde/Ketone → Carboxylic Acid/Derivative → CO₂ (+4).

items.label: Anhydrous PCC vs. Aqueous Jones (CrO₃/H₂SO₄)
items.text: PCC in CH₂Cl₂ stops cleanly at the ALDEHYDE on 1° alcohols; aqueous CrO₃ or KMnO₄ hydrates the aldehyde and oxidizes it to –COOH.

items.label: NaBH₄ vs. LiAlH₄ Hydride Reactivity
items.text: Mild NaBH₄ reduces ONLY aldehydes and ketones (plus acid chlorides); fierce LiAlH₄ reduces aldehydes, ketones, esters, acids, and amides!

comparison: No α-OH C–H left to oxidize further

visualCard.title: Which Oxidant or Reductant Matches Your Target Transformation?
visualCard.prompt: Select your starting material and desired redox product:

items.label: 1° Alcohol → Stop at Aldehyde (RCHO)
items.text: Without water, no geminal diol (hydrate) can form, so oxidation halts cleanly at the aldehyde stage.

items.label: 1° Alcohol or Aldehyde → Carboxylic Acid (RCOOH)
items.text: Water forms the geminal diol RCH(OH)₂, which has a second C–H bond for chromate to oxidize to –COOH.

items.label: Reduce Ketone/Aldehyde in Presence of an Ester
items.text: NaBH₄ selectively reduces the more electrophilic ketone/aldehyde while leaving the ester untouched!

payload.title: Organic oxidation and reduction
payload.fullNote: NaBH4 commonly reduces aldehydes and ketones but ordinarily not esters or carboxylic acids. LiAlH4 reduces esters and acids to alcohols and amides to amines, using suitable nonaqueous reaction conditions followed by a separate workup. Reagent, solvent and workup matter; do not treat LiAlH4 as compatible with an aqueous reaction medium.

visualCard.title: Oxidizing a 3° Alcohol with CrO₃ or Reducing an Ester with NaBH₄

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Drawing a ketone product from a 3° alcohol + CrO₃, or using NaBH₄ to reduce a carboxylic acid or ester.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Oxidation of an alcohol to C=O requires breaking a C–H bond on the carbinol carbon (3° alcohols have zero!), and esters/acids require LiAlH₄.

visualCard.title: NAD⁺ / NADH Biological Hydride Transfer & Alcohol Dehydrogenase

items.label: NAD⁺ ⇌ NADH + H⁺
items.text: NAD⁺ accepts a hydride (H:⁻) to oxidize alcohols to carbonyls; NADH delivers a hydride to reduce carbonyls (e.g., pyruvate → lactate).

items.label: FAD ⇌ FADH₂
items.text: Flavin cofactors oxidize saturated C–C single bonds to conjugated alkenes (e.g., succinate → fumarate in the TCA cycle).

items.label: Disulfide Bridge Redox
items.text: Extracellular oxidizing environments link cysteine thiols into disulfides; cytosolic glutathione keeps thiols reduced.

payload.title: Chemoselectivity and a reaction workflow
payload.fullNote: Inventory functional groups, identify reagent roles, locate the likely reactive site, account for solvent and acid–base steps, then track bonds and stereochemistry. Chemoselectivity means preferential reaction at one functional group.

visualCard.title: Chemo-, Regio-, and Stereoselectivity & The SN1/SN2/E1/E2 Competition Grid

items.label: Chemoselectivity (Functional Group Choice)
items.text: Exploits intrinsic reactivity differences (e.g., Aldehyde > Ketone > Ester toward nucleophiles) or uses protecting groups.

items.label: Regioselectivity (Constitutional Site Choice)
items.text: Determines which positional isomer forms (e.g., small base EtO⁻ gives Zaitsev internal alkene; bulky t-BuO⁻ gives Hofmann less-substituted alkene).

items.label: Stereoselectivity & Stereospecificity
items.text: Stereoselective reactions favor the more stable stereoisomer (E > Z); stereospecific reactions map starting geometry directly to product (SN2 inversion, anti-E2).

visualCard.title: Master Substitution vs. Elimination Decision Engine
visualCard.prompt: Given an alkyl halide RX, how do you predict SN2 vs SN1 vs E2 vs E1?

items.label: Strong Unhindered Nucleophile (CN⁻, RS⁻, I⁻) + 1°/2° RX
items.text: Low basicity + minimal steric hindrance attacks the α-carbon σ* orbital cleanly.

items.label: Strong Base (HO⁻, RO⁻ on 2°/3° RX) OR Bulky Base (t-BuO⁻, LDA)
items.text: Strong bases abstract a β-proton; small bases give the more substituted Zaitsev alkene, while t-BuO⁻ gives the Hofmann alkene.

items.label: Weak Base/Nu (H₂O, ROH) + 3° RX
items.text: Both share the same rate-determining carbocation step; higher temperature (Δ) favors E1 via entropy (TΔS).

payload.title: Chemoselectivity and a reaction workflow
payload.fullNote: Do not substitute a naming-priority or carbon-oxidation-state ranking for reaction analysis. An ester is senior to a ketone in naming, yet its alkoxy oxygen donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance. Under ordinary NaBH4 conditions, the ketone can be reduced while the ester survives. An amide is also resonance-stabilized. Acid–base reactions, activation and conditions can change which site reacts first.

visualCard.title: Confusing Regioselectivity with Chemoselectivity or Stereoselectivity

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Calling Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov addition "chemoselective" or "stereoselective".

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Different atom connectivity (1-ol vs 2-ol, or internal vs terminal alkene) is REGIOSELECTIVE; different 3D arrangement (R/S or E/Z) is STEREOSELECTIVE.

payload.title: Chemoselectivity and a reaction workflow
payload.fullNote: Acetals protect aldehyde/ketone carbonyls from many basic and nucleophilic conditions; aqueous acid restores the carbonyl. Protection replaces the carbonyl pi system with a different functional group, changing electronic reactivity rather than merely adding steric bulk. Carbonyl compounds may also react through acidic alpha hydrogens: deprotonation creates an enolate nucleophile instead of nucleophilic addition at the carbonyl carbon.

visualCard.title: Multi-Step Synthesis Planning & Enzyme Active-Site Specificity

items.label: Protecting Group Strategy
items.outcome: Mask More Reactive FG as Acetal
items.text: To reduce an ester in a keto-ester with LiAlH₄, first protect the ketone as a cyclic acetal (ethylene glycol, H⁺), reduce, then deprotect.

items.label: Thermal Elimination Bias
items.text: Elimination splits 2 particles into 3 particles (↑ ΔS > 0), so raising T makes −TΔS more negative.

items.label: Enzyme Active Sites
items.text: Chiral enzyme pockets hold substrates in a single orientation, achieving 100% selectivity without protecting groups.

payload.title: Analyzing Organic Reactions

lessonInventory.title: Acid–base reasoning
lessonInventory.tag: Equilibrium favors the weaker acid/base pair
lessonInventory.coreRule:
Brønsted acids donate H+ and bases accept it. Lewis acids accept an electron pair; Lewis bases donate one. In a coordinate covalent bond, both shared electrons originate from the donor; the resulting bond is still covalent. For HA + B ⇌ A− + BH+, K ≈ 10^[pKa(BH+) − pKa(HA)] when the pKa values use comparable conditions.
Amphoteric species can act as acids or bases, depending on the partner. Water can accept H+ to form H3O+ or donate H+ to form OH−; bicarbonate can likewise gain or lose a proton.

lessonInventory.title: Nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups
lessonInventory.tag: Electron pairs move from donor to acceptor
lessonInventory.coreRule: A nucleophile supplies an electron pair to an electrophile. A leaving group takes the bonding pair when it departs. Stable weak bases usually make better leaving groups. Protonation can turn poor leaving group OH− into neutral water.

lessonInventory.title: SN1 vs. SN2
lessonInventory.tag: Mechanism depends on substrate and conditions
lessonInventory.coreRule: SN2 is concerted backside attack: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile], with geometric inversion. Methyl and unhindered primary centers are favorable. SN1 ionizes to a carbocation: rate = k[substrate]; tertiary, allylic, and benzylic stabilization can help.

lessonInventory.title: Organic oxidation and reduction
lessonInventory.tag: Track bonds to H and electronegative atoms
lessonInventory.coreRule: Oxidation of carbon usually increases bonds to O/N/halogens or decreases C–H bonds. Reduction does the reverse. C–C bonds contribute zero to carbon oxidation state. PCC under anhydrous conditions can oxidize a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Aqueous acidic CrO3 or dichromate (Na2Cr2O7/K2Cr2O7), or suitable KMnO4 conditions, can oxidize a primary alcohol further to a carboxylic acid; substrate and conditions determine the outcome.

lessonInventory.title: Chemoselectivity and a reaction workflow
lessonInventory.tag: Choose by reactivity, not naming seniority
lessonInventory.coreRule: Inventory functional groups, identify reagent roles, locate the likely reactive site, account for solvent and acid–base steps, then track bonds and stereochemistry. Chemoselectivity means preferential reaction at one functional group.
